articles.title: ‘China, US, Russia consensus positive for HK economy’
articles.excerpt: Commerce Secretary Algernon Yau said on Saturday that the joint declaration of peace issued by President Xi Jinping and his…
articles.fullText:
Commerce Secretary Algernon Yau said on Saturday that the joint declaration of peace issued by President Xi Jinping and his US and Russian counterparts, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin, is positive for the world economy and Hong Kong.

The three leaders released the declaration following trilateral talks on the sidelines of the Apec Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen.

Speaking on RTHK, Yau said the consensus reached by the major powers would support global stability and trade.

"In the meeting between the leaders of China, Russia and the United States, they all hoped to reach a consensus on building a peaceful world, resolving conflicts in the world and creating a prosperous global economy through cooperation," he said.

"The consensus reached by the three major countries will have an impact on the future global economy, including Hong Kong's economy."

During his keynote speech at the Apec CEO Summit, Xi said China supports establishing a world association for bay area economic cooperation to deepen exchanges between such areas and strengthen Asia-Pacific economic ties.

Yau said that as a key city in the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area, Hong Kong plays a vital role in helping the region connect with other bay areas worldwide, such as those in Japan and the United States.

The SAR can contribute, he said, by leveraging its advantages as an international centre for trade, shipping and finance.

"I think the opportunities are enormous," Yau said.

"If these bay areas can connect and boost trade, it will greatly expand import-export activity, personnel exchanges and talent complementarity."

During the Apec summit, Chief Executive John Lee also held bilateral talks with leaders from seven economies: Malaysia, Vietnam, Brunei, Thailand, Chile, Peru and Singapore.

Yau said the discussions focused on cooperation in areas such as education and trade, while also touching on tariffs and the avoidance of double taxation.

He said the chief executive also briefed the leaders about opportunities in the Northern Metropolis.

In meetings with leaders from Asean members, Lee also discussed Hong Kong's bid to join the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership, Yau added.

Edited by Robert Kemp

articles.title: Grand Theft Auto rakes in almost US$3.8bn on first day
articles.excerpt: "Grand Theft Auto VI" brought in US$3.79 billion in retail sales on its first day, publisher Rockstar Games said on…
articles.fullText:
"Grand Theft Auto VI" brought in US$3.79 billion in retail sales on its first day, publisher Rockstar Games said on Friday, calling it the biggest launch for any entertainment product in history.

The figure, based on company estimates of worldwide sales through the end of Thursday, is nearly five times the roughly US$800 million that predecessor "Grand Theft Auto V" took in during its first 24 hours in 2013.

Rockstar, a label of New York-based Take-Two Interactive, said the game had sold 32.5 million units before release, a record across all platforms.

"We are incredibly humbled by the response from players around the world," said Sam Houser, the studio's founder and president.

The game came out on Thursday on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S. It launched first at midnight in New Zealand and then rolled out to each market as the clock reached midnight there.

The release generated more social media posts than this year's World Cup, according to monitoring platform Visibrain.

Critics praised the game, which has a score of 99 on review aggregator Metacritic. Rockstar said that made it the highest-rated game ever.

In a review for The Verge, Andrew Webster wrote that "the game is so good that the outsize hype is the least interesting thing about it."

This week the game received eight nominations for the Game Awards, which will be held December 10.

Rockstar spent more than eight years developing the title. It delayed the launch twice, first from autumn 2025 and then from May 2026.

The studio was also hit by a 2022 hack in which stolen gameplay footage was posted online.

The series has long been accused of glorifying violence and crime. (AFP)

Edited by Robert Kemp

articles.title: Harry Kane out 'for months' with ankle injury
articles.excerpt: Ballon d'Or winner Harry Kane is set to be out for "months" with an ankle injury, Bayern Munich coach Vincent…
articles.fullText:
Ballon d'Or winner Harry Kane is set to be out for "months" with an ankle injury, Bayern Munich coach Vincent Kompany said on Friday.

England captain Kane was subbed out early in the Bayern's 1-1 Bundesliga home draw against Cologne after a tackle with Kompany telling Sky Germany the forward would to be out for "months" rather than "weeks". (AFP)

Edited by Robert Kemp

articles.title: Tech stocks slump, leaving Nasdaq in red for the year
articles.excerpt: A bruising sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks on Friday pulled the S&P 500 down 3.7 percent, dragging the index to…
articles.fullText:
A bruising sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks on Friday pulled the S&P 500 down 3.7 percent, dragging the index to its worst weekly loss in more than 18 months, and knocking the Nasdaq composite into the red for the year.

The S&P 500 fell 265.44 points to 6,910.39. The Dow dropped 949.73 points to 48,147.33, and the Nasdaq lost 1,261.47 points to close at 22,617.73.

The benchmark index is now in what professional investors call a “correction,” having fallen more than 10 percent from its Oct. 6 all-time high.

The last time the S&P 500 had a correction was March 2025, as the Trump administration’s trade war rattled the market. Its weekly loss, marking its worst such decline since April 2025, as the trade war escalated, capped a seven-day losing streak, the longest such string of losses since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020.

The Nasdaq composite slumped 5.3 percent, pulling it into negative territory for the year. Its weekly loss was also just shy of its worst week since March 2020.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average, with less exposure to technology stocks, fell 1.9 percent.

Chip stocks like Nvidia, Micron Technology, Broadcom and Advanced Micro Devices bore the brunt of the selling, but other companies connected to the AI buildout tanked as well, including the optical products company Corning and the energy provider Bloom Energy. The AI lab Anthropic, coming off a successful IPO Thursday, tumbled 9.1percent.

The AI trade has been losing steam partly over worries that AI stocks’ big market values and heavy spending are unjustified. Fears of a bubble within the sector have also been exacerbated by the results of the recent midterm elections, with candidates advocating for a slowdown in data centre construction winning at both the federal and state level.

“The whole notion that AI can continue to spend unlimited amounts of money and support the stock market, I think the notion of that is ending as we speak, that’s what’s being priced right now,” said Michael Antonelli, market strategist at Baird. “But I don’t think that means that the overall bull market that started in October 2022 is over.”

Much of the AI rout was centred among chip stocks, which have been big beneficiaries of the build out of AI data centres. Advanced Micro Devices sank 13.3 percent, Micron Technology slid 13.9 percent and Broadcom fell 12.1 percent.

Nvidia, considered by many to be the poster child for the AI boom, fell for the ninth day in the last 10, closing 13.8 percent lower. The chip company’s stock was caught up in the market’s anxiety about the strength of the AI build out, and more recently has been pressured by worries about its future following the sudden downfall of Jensen Huang , its former CEO and co-founder. Since the Huang scandal erupted earlier this month, the stock has dropped more than 25 percent.

The big market debut for Anthropic, maker of the Claude AI tool, fizzled on Friday with the rest of the tech sector. The stock fell 9.1 percent to US$88.30, but remains above its IPO price of US$83 per share. It was the biggest public stock offering ever, at one point surpassing US$2 trillion in value. (AP)

Edited by Robert Kemp

articles.title: UK, EU hail new deals 10 years after Brexit
articles.excerpt: UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham and the EU's top officials on Friday sealed deals at a Brussels summit to ease…
articles.fullText:
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham and the EU's top officials on Friday sealed deals at a Brussels summit to ease trade and youth mobility after Brexit, but kicked down the road the question of where ties go next.

Burnham has re-energised talk of closer ties a decade after Britain voted to leave the European Union, and the mood was upbeat as the prime minister shook hands with EU chiefs Ursula von der Leyen and Antonio Costa.

One potential dampener emerged as the 27-nation bloc and London jostled over linking ultimate implementation of the new deals to Britain agreeing to cut university fees for EU students -- but both sides cast the day as a win.

"This is a good day for Britain. This is a good day for Europe," Burnham told the gathering, hailing a "landmark" agreement -- while the EU's von der Leyen called it a "turning point" in relations.

Wrapped up in Brussels were three main agreements: a deal cutting red tape for food exports, another linking the two sides' emissions-trading schemes and a third on a "youth experience scheme".

Burnham argued the accords -- initiated by his predecessor, Keir Starmer -- will unpick some of the damage inflicted by the "hard Brexit we ended up with" and provide a US$22-billion boost to the British economy.

British firms will export to Europe more easily again and 100,000 under-30s from each side will be allowed to reside for up to three years in the other's territory for work, study or travel.

But while the optics at the meeting may have been much improved, old habits die hard.

Brussels and London wrangled down to the wire over the details of the deals.

One sticking point was on pinning London down to a future agreement on cutting fees for EU students at UK universities to the level paid by their British counterparts.

Burnham insisted that the "deal is done", even if talks would continue on tuition fees over the next six months.

But a statement from EU countries seen by AFP said they would hold off implementation until there was an agreement over the fees.

Since taking power this summer, Burnham has defied the taboos in Britain's toxic debate over Europe -- going as far as to float rejoining the bloc one day.

European Council boss Costa told Burnham the EU was open to having the "closest possible relationship".

But the summit focused on smaller steps, and the prime minister kicked the can on what could come next.

Having previously said he would like to see Britain rejoin the EU in his lifetime, Burnham has promised to lay out options that could range from leaving things as they are to entering the customs union or becoming a member again.

He said he would hold an "informal brainstorming" with the EU over the next year to look at options.

"We do need to consider what is the right long-term relationship. Incremental steps, as you say, only take us so far," Burnham said in response to a question from AFP -- while conceding Friday's deals were likely "the limit of what we can achieve in this parliament".

"The British people will be the boss of what happens next. We will not be running ahead of public opinion," he said.

Burnham hopes friendlier EU relations will help build a broad centre-left coalition to win the next general election, not anticipated until 2029.

Polls now regularly indicate most Britons regret Brexit.

However, Burnham's own party is divided on how to proceed.

The Labour leader's push leaves him open to accusations of Brexit betrayal from the opposition Conservatives and hard-right Reform UK party of Nigel Farage -- who shadowed Burnham to Brussels and delivered his own press conference.

"He's let the genie out of the bottle, and I think he's going to be very, very surprised by the backlash he gets," Farage told journalists. (AFP)

Edited by Robert Kemp

articles.title: The most misunderstood graph in AI just got a major update
articles.excerpt: A new report from the AI evaluation nonprofit METR finds that some AI capabilities are continuing to improve along an…
articles.fullText:
A new report from the AI evaluation nonprofit METR finds that some AI capabilities are continuing to improve along an exponential trajectory—but it also indicates that models aren’t quite as good at tasks that require judgment as they are at coding. 

The report is an update to the organization’s time horizon plot, which was widely shared— and widely misinterpreted , owing to the complexity of the measures it used. METR evaluated models by having them attempt a large suite of tasks, each of which had also been completed by humans. Each task’s difficulty was scored by how long it took the human testers to finish it—and then models were rated according to the length of the tasks that they could complete. That plot showed that AI systems were rapidly improving—every four months, the length of the tasks that frontier models could successfully complete doubled.

The updated plot adds more tasks—some that are estimated to take humans far longer than those in the original suite, and others that are more open-ended. One of the biggest questions in AI right now is the extent to which progress on “verifiable” tasks—where it’s possible to check automatically whether an AI system has succeeded or failed—carry over into tasks on which success or failure is harder to measure. We know how to teach neural networks how to do verifiable tasks: Researchers have the systems attempt one many times, strengthen the neural pathways that contribute to success, and weaken the pathways that contribute to failures. That’s why AI systems have become so good at coding and math, two domains where it’s possible to determine automatically whether a solution does or doesn’t work.

It’s much harder to apply this technique, known as reinforcement learning, to tasks where success is less well defined or takes longer to ascertain—such as choosing a new research direction. For the same reason, it’s tough to evaluate AI performance on these tasks, so METR’s original time horizon plot didn’t include any of them. But it’s precisely this type of task that will prove essential if AI systems are to automate research and development.

And AI research and development is an especially hot topic right now. Parts of the AI community are still reeling from a different, heavily redacted METR report from earlier this month, which claimed that AI might be speeding up the pace of AI progress at Anthropic by a factor of two. That report sparked fears that the company (which just had a blockbuster IPO) could soon achieve full recursive self-improvement, a regime in which AI systems autonomously design their own successors with no human involvement.

METR researchers have worked to make sure their new suite of tasks includes some of the fuzzier, judgment-laden ones that could be most relevant to AI research and development. In one task, they ask models to design new AI evaluations that METR could use in its research and then have human METR employees score the results. Even though the most advanced models are now better than almost every human at software engineering, here they fall short: Not one of the AI-designed evaluations was good enough for METR employees to consider it useful for their research.

In another task, models have to score philosophical arguments. This task is intended to capture the extent to which models can exercise good judgment—though METR writes in the report that employees disagree about how relevant the task is for automation of AI R&D. On this task, too, models fell short of human performance.

Though it’s difficult to score these new tasks—and even harder to determine what the scores mean—experts I spoke with appreciate that METR is incorporating new types of evaluations into its work. “We’re at the point where AI evaluations need to get more creative,” says Sayash Kapoor, a computer scientist and incoming professor at UC Berkeley. “Trying to push the envelope of the space of evaluations is a welcome change.”

Kapoor says he wasn’t surprised to see that models fall short of performance on more open-ended tasks, such as designing an AI evaluation—in a preprint from August , he and his collaborators reported that AI models are not yet able to reproduce human computer science research on their own. And in a Wednesday blog post, OpenAI reported that its models don’t do as well on the real-world tasks its employees assign them as they do on the easier, more verifiable tasks in METR’s original suite.

Still, people disagree about how to interpret current performance differences on easily verifiable and hard-to-verify tasks, Kapoor says. Though he thinks that research taste—the ability to choose promising questions, hypotheses, and experiments—will prove a major bottleneck in automating AI R&D, others contend that models trained on easy-to-verify tasks will eventually be able to successfully complete open-ended tasks as well. And progress on verifiable tasks doesn’t seem to be slowing down.

Even if the models do lag behind human performance on open-ended tasks right now, the new report suggests that they might be getting better. Some of the newest models, such as Opus 5.5, tend to achieve what METR calls “borderline above the bar” performance on the evaluation design tasks—not yet usable for METR’s research, but promising. Just a year ago, every model was scoring in the “clearly below the bar” category.

But because these open-ended and judgment-heavy tasks are so tough to design and score, METR includes few of them in its report, and that makes it difficult to predict whether and how models might continue to progress in these areas. “The improvement we observe, I think that does tell us something for the current moment,” says Najoung Kim, a linguist and computer scientist at Boston University. “I’m not sure just yet how to think about how it would extrapolate.”

Matt Putz, a member of the technical staff at METR, says that predicting progress on these kinds of tasks is likely to remain difficult. “By their nature, hard-to-verify or judgment-laden tasks are much harder to study, and especially to quantify,” he said in an email. “Ultimately, I don’t think we’ll be able to establish trends as clean and robust as for the easy-to-specify [tasks].”

In general, METR is clearly butting up against the practical difficulties of testing AI performance on difficult and underspecified tasks—precisely the ones most relevant to automating AI R&D. METR’s time horizon plots score task difficulty by evaluating how long it would take a human to complete the task, and for the original plot they measured this quantity by actually having people try each task.

In the new report, however, the completion times are mostly estimates, because paying people for tasks that might take hundreds of hours, or that only a few experts are qualified to complete, is prohibitively expensive and time-consuming. Other tasks have more specific shortcomings—for example, for the philosophical argument task, just one person rated most of the arguments, and agents are judged by how well they agree with that particular individual. It’s possible that the scores would change if more experts were surveyed—but that, too, is time-consuming.

It’s still early days for evaluating models on tasks that are hard to validate or require judgment. And while the experts I spoke with see the inclusion of these tasks in METR’s newest time horizon plot as a clear step in the right direction, they agree that we are still far from achieving any definitive answers about whether, and how quickly, automated AI R&D might be coming. “This move toward open-ended tasks is promising,” Kapoor says. But, he adds, “there is just such a lot more to be done to actually get a fuller understanding.”

articles.title: Global praise for HK infrastructure
articles.excerpt: InfraEX Week 2026 opened yesterday with its flagship event – the 2nd International Infrastructure and Projects Leaders Summit – bringing…
articles.fullText:
InfraEX Week 2026 opened yesterday with its flagship event – the 2nd International Infrastructure and Projects Leaders Summit – bringing together leading experts and professionals from over 30 countries and regions.

Participants praised the summit’s strong global appeal and shared positive views on Hong Kong’s ongoing infrastructure development.

Ashghal Technical Office Assistant Manager Hayat Bukshaisha said that Hong Kong has strong experience in planning and delivering major infrastructure projects.

“We are taking Hong Kong as a benchmark. We look to Hong Kong and learn from past experience, especially when it comes to modern methods of construction and project delivery,” she said.

Deloitte Australia Senior Partner Sean McClowry noted that he is particularly interested in the Northern Metropolis Project.

“It is one of the most exciting initiatives of its kind in the world, and seeing this kind of greenfield initiative coming to life is really exciting for me,” he said. “Always when I come to Hong Kong, just seeing how the infrastructure works together and how you fuse physical infrastructure and digital technologies is very interesting to me.”

Ministry of Finance of the Republic of Singapore Executive Director (Centre for Public Project Management) Low Chian Siong highlighted the value of opportunities that he gained by joining the event.

“The greatest takeaway for me is not just learning what other participants are doing, but also actually the network that we create and continue to maintain,” he said.

He said he was also amazed by how much Hong Kong has achieved in a very short time in terms of planning and execution.

Meanwhile, Professor Tarek Zayed of The Hong Kong Polytechnic University Department of Construction Management & Intelligence, who has spent nine years working in Hong Kong, emphasised the city’s high standards in infrastructure.

“I have been in contact with many departments in Hong Kong and doing a lot of research in many infrastructures including bridges, tunnels, water networks, sewer networks, highways or pavement. The infrastructure here is strong, very good, and many of them are new, very sustainable and resilient for the coming generation.”

Association of Consulting Engineers of Hong Kong Chairman Ole Wong said that the summit encourages valuable exchanges with overseas professionals.

“We can share, we can collaborate and we think about an integrated opportunity with each other together. So the summit is very successful and we hope we can meet as many leaders as possible from different places. We can all work together and we can think about our future, embrace our challenges together,” he said.

articles.title: How a temple on a rock became a monument
articles.excerpt: Wan Chai’s Queen’s Road East is a bustling thoroughfare lined with towering skyscrapers, yet sitting quietly in a corner of…
articles.fullText:
Wan Chai’s Queen’s Road East is a bustling thoroughfare lined with towering skyscrapers, yet sitting quietly in a corner of this urban hub is a historic temple. Built between 1847 and 1852, Hung Shing Temple has endured for nearly 180 years and was officially declared a monument by the Government in October 2026.

Shifting shorelines
Dedicated to Hung Shing, the God of the South Sea widely worshipped by fishermen and merchant seafarers, the temple has deep maritime roots – making its current inland setting seem puzzling at first glance.

Development Bureau Antiquities & Monuments Office Curator (Historic Buildings) Alice Yu explained the mystery: “Hung Shing Temple was originally built on the shoreline of Hong Kong Island. The two streets opposite the temple – Tai Wong Street East and Tai Wong Street West – are both named after the temple's popular name, Tai Wong.”

Through decades of land reclamation and urban development, the sea that once stretched before the temple has given way to busy streets and high-rises. Today, the temple serves as a historical landmark, silently chronicling Wan Chai’s shifting coastline.

Lingnan craftsmanship
Beyond its historical significance, Hung Shing Temple stands out as an architectural gem in the Lingnan style. It features a traditional single-hall, three-bay layout, complete with an elevated entrance porch and an unusual side-access design.

Exquisite granite columns carved with human figures and "prawn-shaped" tie beams support the porch, while granite balustrades – centred around an intricate double-dragon-and-pearl motif – frame the entrance. Crowning the roof are ornate Shiwan ridge decorations from 1909, depicting the legendary heroine Fan Lihua.

Stepping inside reveals the building's most astonishing architectural feature: the temple was built directly onto a natural rock formation. Ms Yu noted that the rock merges seamlessly with the structure, becoming part of the temple itself.

“This kind of structure, which adapts to the terrain and features a coexistence between the temple and the rock formation, is quite rare among temples in Hong Kong,” she said. “The temple walls had to follow the uneven and irregular surface of the rock, demonstrating the craftsmanship and architectural wisdom of tailoring (a structure) to local conditions.”

Shared devotion
That the temple has survived in remarkably original condition for nearly two centuries is a testament to the dedicated care of generations of local residents and caretakers. Following major expansions and upgrades in 1860 and 1867 – heavily backed by the Chinese community and a local quarry firm – the temple flourished.

In the past, worshippers placed ancestral soul tablets inside the temple. Over time, it gradually welcomed a variety of deities, including Lady Kam Fa for safe childbirth and Lady Fa Fan for eternal youth, as well as Man Cheong, Wah To and Tai Sui – reflecting the inclusive, multi-deity nature of Chinese folk beliefs.

Living heritage
In the face of changing times, the temple’s management has introduced fresh initiatives in recent years to connect traditional heritage with younger generations. Tung Wah Group of Hospitals Senior Manager (Temple & Cultural Services) Vandesar Leung noted that while preserving traditional worship services, the organisation is committed to hosting events, as well as developing cultural and creative products.

“We aim to attract more citizens and visitors to discover Hung Shing Temple through guided tours, education programmes and cultural promotion. By offering workshops and lectures, and including the temple in tour routes, we highlight how Hung Shing worship connects with fishing village history and Wan Chai’s growth.”

“More than a historic building, the temple is a living cultural witness,” he said.

From a modest shrine on a bygone shoreline to a declared monument in the heart of a modern metropolis, Hung Shing Temple in Wan Chai does more than record a community's faith and transformation. It stands as a living bridge between past and future – safeguarding the historical memory of this city.

articles.title: Spain and France clash in Nations League quarter-final
articles.excerpt: World champions Spain will face France, while England will play Norway in the quarter-finals of the UEFA Nations League, after…
articles.fullText:
World champions Spain will face France, while England will play Norway in the quarter-finals of the UEFA Nations League, after the draw took place on Friday.

Spain beat France 2-0 in the semi-finals of the World Cup in the United States in July, on the way to winning the trophy. They also defeated Les Bleus 5-4 in the semi-finals of the last edition of the Nations League, last year.

"This will not be about getting revenge for the World Cup semi-final," Zinedine Zidane, who was appointed France coach following that tournament, told L'Equipe.

"We knew we were going to get a strong opponent and we have got the reigning world champions."

The quarter-finals will be played over two legs in late March, with Spain at home first after coming second in Group A3, while France topped Group A1.

Spain won the Nations League in 2023, while France beat them to win the 2021 final.

England topped Group A3 on goal difference after beating Spain away in their last outing, and their reward is a two-legged last-eight tie against Norway with the first leg on Norwegian soil.

England edged Norway in the World Cup quarter-finals this year before losing to Argentina in the semi-finals.

The other quarter-final ties pitched reigning Nations League champions Portugal against the Netherlands, and Belgium against Germany.

"So much can happen in the time between now and then," Germany coach Jurgen Klopp told the German team's in-house broadcaster, DFB TV.

"We're very happy with the last impression we left, but we're also fully aware that we are right at the beginning of a development process," added Klopp, whose team topped Group A2 after thrashing the Netherlands 5-0 in Berlin on Monday.

"We want to carry this positive momentum forward. There's still a great deal of work to be done."

The winners of the quarter-finals will advance to the final stages, which will be held in June in a venue yet to be decided.

Spain or France will play the Netherlands or Portugal in the semis, with England facing Belgium or Germany should they get past Norway.

The Nations League quarter-finals and play-offs in March will all take place at the same time as qualifying begins for Euro 2028. (AFP)

Edited by Raymond Yeung

articles.title: COP31 deal elusive as fossil fuel fight deepens
articles.excerpt: The UN's COP31 climate talks were set to spill into overtime Friday as countries remained deadlocked over a draft deal…
articles.fullText:
The UN's COP31 climate talks were set to spill into overtime Friday as countries remained deadlocked over a draft deal that makes no mention of fossil fuels, with a host of other disputes also snarling negotiations.

Grey skies added to the sombre mood in the Turkish Mediterranean city of Antalya as negotiators from nearly 200 countries struggled to bridge their differences after two weeks of intense talks, which could now run into the weekend.

"At this point, no one is happy," Brazil's national secretary for climate change, Aloisio Lopes Pereira de Melo, told reporters with only hours before the conference's official end.

The talks come with a series of stark reminders of the urgency of climate action, from heatwaves in Europe and devastating floods in Nepal, while a record-breaking El Nino -- a periodic warming pattern -- supercharges temperatures.

But expectations for a major breakthrough are low at COP31 as countries cope with an oil price shock and geopolitical tensions stemming from the war in Iran.

A sprawling initial draft deal earlier this week called for accelerating the phase-out of fossil fuels, along with other flashpoint topics such as finance and climate science.

But a new, shorter version released by COP31 co-host Australia on Thursday omitted any mention of the main drivers of climate change, sparking calls for the language to be restored.

Instead, the draft "cover decision" calls for electrifying the world economy, saying it could have "significant benefits" in shoring up energy security and cutting planet-heating greenhouse gas emissions.

The text reflects a push by COP31 host Turkey for countries to rally behind a goal to increase the global share of final energy demand met by electricity to 35 percent by 2035.

But some countries want the text to call for "clean" electrification to make clear that renewables, not coal or gas, must be the energy source.

Nations agreed at COP28 in Dubai in 2023 to transition away from fossil fuels, without setting targets or timelines, but Saudi Arabia and other major oil producers have fiercely resisted any attempt to bring the issue back to the table.

A dozen European and developing countries -- from France to Panama and the Solomon Islands -- released a letter insisting that the text include "a clear transition away from fossil fuels".

Panama's environment minister, Juan Carlos Navarro, said "the COP can still be saved" if the deal includes the phase-out and other issues, including a defence of climate science.

An outspoken critic of what he calls the "petroleum mafia", Navarro has threatened to block any deal that does not include a cap on oil production.

A European Union official, speaking on condition of anonymity, told AFP that the latest draft was "not acceptable and not ambitious enough".

"We don't want this COP to become a 'fossil' COP," the official said.

Countries are sharply divided over a raft of other issues.

A fight over the timing of the next set of reports by the UN's Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) has been a major source of friction.

The draft also expresses "deep concern" about the imminent breach of the 1.5-degree Celsius goal set under the 2015 Paris accord.

Negotiations are also deadlocked over long-running complaints by developing countries that rich nations are falling short in their obligations to help them confront climate change.

"We didn't come here to beg," said Ghana's environment minister, Zanetor Agyeman-Rawlings.

"The (African) continent will not accept an outcome that offers declarations without the resources to deliver them," she said. (AFP)

Edited by Raymond Yeung

articles.title: The Download: inside the quest to make our minds immortal
articles.excerpt: This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in…
articles.fullText:
This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.

What we learned when our Roundtables explored the quest to make minds immortal

To preserve our sense of self, some scientists are working on ways to keep our brains going—even beyond death. In their quest for cognitive immortality, these “mind savers” are exploring everything from head transplants and brain freezing to conscious software avatars.

In the latest MIT Technology Review Roundtables event, senior editor for biomedicine Antonio Regalado joined science editor Mary Beth Griggs to examine these ideas. After following the money, the science, and the philosophy, he came back part skeptical, part awestruck. Here’s a taste of what Antonio found—and what he made of it.

- Not all the projects are quite what they seem: A $190 million US government program to develop replacement brain tissue is officially about treating stroke, but “it’s also a fig leaf for the actual ambition”: living forever.

- AI could lead to convincing mind clones: Large language models are making it possible to build AI copies of people that act quite like the real thing. “This digital avatar might not be good enough for you, but what if it’s good enough for me?”

- Immortality can be a hard sell: One company, Nectome, wants to preserve brains within 12 minutes of medically assisted death. “If you’re selling a hot product, this is not it.”

- It’s not always clear what we’re trying to preserve: “I’m not even sure that I have a very good claim to be myself.”

- There’s an upside to life as a brain in a jar: “You can surf the internet. I do that pretty much 12 hours a day, anyway.”

To find out which of these ideas might actually work, subscribers can now watch the full conversation on demand .

Want to join the conversation? Subscribe to MIT Technology Review for exclusive access to all our Roundtables.

The must-reads

articles.title: Top seed Wang Zhiyi through to HK Badminton Open semis
articles.excerpt: China's top seed Wang Zhiyi advanced to the women's singles semifinals at the Hong Kong Open Badminton Championships 2026 on…
articles.fullText:
China's top seed Wang Zhiyi advanced to the women's singles semifinals at the Hong Kong Open Badminton Championships 2026 on Friday, while men's doubles stars Liang Weikeng and Wang Chang bowed out in the quarterfinals.

Wang edged sixth seed Putri Kusuma Wardani of Indonesia 22-20, 22-20 in a tightly contested match.

After clinching a close opening game, Wang led 18-15 in the second before Wardani reeled off five straight points to reach game point. Keeping her composure under pressure, the Chinese shuttler responded with four consecutive points to seal the victory in straight games.

"When I dropped five points in a row and fell behind in the second game, I told myself to stay calm and focused, and make adjustments," Wang said.

In the men's doubles, Liang and Wang, silver medalists at the 2024 Paris Olympics, fell to South Korean duo Kang Min-hyuk and Lee Jong-min 19-21, 21-19, 18-21.

Fellow Chinese pair Hu Keyuan and Lin Xiangyi also exited the tournament, losing 2-1 to Hangzhou Asian Games champions Satwiksairaj Rankireddy and Chirag Shetty of India.

In mixed doubles, top seeds Feng Yanzhe and Huang Dongping needed just 26 minutes to eliminate Chinese Taipei's Wu Hsuan-yi and Yang Chu-yun in straight games.

"We prepared thoroughly for a tough battle and executed our game plan well, preventing our opponents from finding any way to restrict us," Huang said.

Second seeds Jiang Zhenbang and Wei Yaxin also cruised into the mixed doubles semifinals.

The Hong Kong Open is part of the BWF World Tour Super 500 and runs from November 17 to 22. (Xinhua)

Edited by Raymond Yeung

articles.title: Govt going all out to help Wang Fuk residents: CS
articles.excerpt: The government is doing everything it can to help residents of Wang Fuk Court to move on and start a…
articles.fullText:
The government is doing everything it can to help residents of Wang Fuk Court to move on and start a new life, Chief Secretary Eric Chan said on Friday.

Ahead of the one-year anniversary of the fire that killed 168 people at the Tai Po housing estate, Chan stressed that the public can freely attend memorial events so long as they are legal.

Responding to reporters' questions after officiating at the opening ceremony of a Community Living Room in North Point, Chan said he had heard that certain groups were being pressured to cancel certain memorial activities.

"I would like to clarify here and reiterate that Hong Kong is governed by the rule of law. Any memorial activities, as long as they are legal, are absolutely permitted by the government," he said, citing examples such as events held by religious bodies.

But he urged the public to be careful in choosing which events to attend, saying there are individuals with ulterior motives who wish to use this opportunity to create trouble.

"I want to remind our citizens that when participating in such memorial events, they must be careful in their choices and make sure not to be taken advantage of by people with hidden agendas," he said.

If in doubt, Chan suggested the public enquire with the government.

The chief secretary said that the government, led by Chief Executive John Lee, had been going all out to assist residents affected by the fire, including rehousing them as soon as possible.

But most importantly, he said, is how reforms must be implemented to prevent a repeat of the disaster, citing ongoing legislative amendments to minimise fire risks and stamp out bid-rigging in building maintenance projects.

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: Hong Kong inflation remains moderate at 2.2pc
articles.excerpt: Hong Kong's consumer inflation remained moderate in October, with overall prices rising by 2.2 percent year on year. The figure…
articles.fullText:
Hong Kong's consumer inflation remained moderate in October, with overall prices rising by 2.2 percent year on year.

The figure, published by the Census and Statistics Department on Friday, compared with the 1.9 percent expansion in September, although the government attributed the larger increase last month to the end of the rates concession.

For the first 10 months of 2026, the composite consumer price index (CPI) rose by 1.8 percent over the same period a year ago.

Netting out the effects of the government's one-off relief measures, the underlying inflation in October stood at two percent, compared to 2.1 percent in September.

Breaking down the various components of the composite CPI, prices jumped by 12.7 percent for electricity, gas and water and 11.4 percent for health services.

Transport costs, which are sensitive to rising fuel prices, increased by 4.5 percent.

There were milder increases for necessities such as food, which edged up by 0.3 percent, while housing rents ticked up 1.4 percent.

A government spokesman noted that the prices of fuel-related items continued to rise noticeably.

"But spillover effects remained limited, with prices of most other items increasing modestly or declining," he said.

Looking ahead, the spokesman said price pressures on other fronts should remain broadly in check, although geopolitical tensions remain a key source of near-term uncertainty for international fuel prices.

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: Seven arrested for allegedly smuggling in nine animals
articles.excerpt: Customs officers on Friday said they arrested seven people, three men and four women, aged between 33 and 56, for…
articles.fullText:
Customs officers on Friday said they arrested seven people, three men and four women, aged between 33 and 56, for allegedly trying to smuggle nine animals into Hong Kong through the Sha Tau Kok Control Point.

The animals — seven cats and two dogs — had an estimated total market value of about HK$92,000.

Senior Investigator Li tsz-wing said in one case, the crime syndicate first placed the animals in plastic bags and smuggled them into Hong Kong through Chung Ying Street in Sha Tau Kok, before transferring them using two privates cars to a location outside a shopping mall in Tuen Mun for handover.

He said the suspects were arrested at the scene and further arrests were made the day after.

“Investigations found that these criminal syndicates often use circuitous methods involving multiple transfers to avoid detection by our officers,” he said.

"They first arrange for couriers to smuggle the animals across the border, then quickly transfer them using different vehicles within a short period of time, before finally handing them over to buyers or recipients in Hong Kong. This is done to complicate tracing efforts for our officers.”

Li said that in another case, a man was seen allegedly smuggling five cats and two puppies on his bicycle and in his personal luggage at Sha Tau Kok Border Control Point and was arrested at the scene.

Li noted that all animals involved were handed over to the Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department for further investigation.

Following the incident, customs officials reminded the public that it is an offence to import animals into the SAR without a valid permit.

Under the Rabies Regulation, anyone found guilty of illegally importing animals is liable to a fine up to HK$50,000 and imprisonment for one year.

Customs officials also warned the public to stay vigilant against unscrupulous online pet sellers.

It said anyone involved in importing animals without a valid permit — including buyers, sellers, transporters, or recipients — faces criminal liability.

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: Public housing wait falls to decade low of 4.4 years
articles.excerpt: The latest composite waiting time for subsidised rental housing has fallen to 4.4 years, a 10-year low and a drop…
articles.fullText:
The latest composite waiting time for subsidised rental housing has fallen to 4.4 years, a 10-year low and a drop of 0.4 years from 4.8 years at the end of June, the Housing Bureau said on Friday.

The figure, it said, is 1.7 years below the peak of 6.1 years before the current-term government took office and the first time it has fallen below four-and-a-half years.

The composite waiting time (CWT) is based on the average waiting time of general applicants housed to public rental housing or light public housing in the 12 months to the end of September 2026.

A bureau spokesman said the long-standing backlogged applications have been gradually cleared with rising overall public housing production and the progressive completion of various projects, producing a downward trend.

"We are confident that we can achieve the target of reducing the CWT to 4.5 years in 2026-27 as announced by the chief executive in the 2022 Policy Address," he said.

The bureau said public housing production is entering a harvesting phase.

In the next five years, from 2027-28 to 2031-32, more than 35,000 units per year on average will be provided, about 73 percent more than in the five years since the current-term government took office, the highest in 25 years.

On light public housing, about 29,800 units had been completed as of the middle of this November, with the remaining two projects, converted from school premises in Kwun Tong and Wong Tai Sin, providing about 210 units upon completion in the first quarter of next year.

All 13 projects providing about 30,000 units will be completed in slightly over four years, ahead of the five-year target.

In the third quarter of this year, about 11,200 general applicants were housed in public rental housing or light public housing, including about 3,100 newly completed flats, about 2,700 recovered flats and about 5,450 light public housing units, with the last figure being more than four times that of the previous quarter.

The spokesman said the average quarterly supply over the past 12 months rose to about 8,200 units, double the average of about 4,100 units in the four years before the current-term government took office.

The waiting time for general applicants housed in public rental housing over the period was 5.3 years, while for those housed in light public housing it was only 2.8 years on average, showing the policy has played a key role in enabling faster fulfilment of grassroots housing needs.

The bureau also said the public rental housing waiting queue had hit a 15-year low.

As of the end of September, there were about 96,100 general applications, down nearly 40 percent from the peak of 156,400 in September 2020 and the first time the figure had fallen below 100,000 since 2012.

Non-elderly one-person applications fell by over 40 percent from their peak, with the decline among those aged below 30 even more pronounced, dropping about 60 percent over the past decade to about 29,300.

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: HK, mainland slip as tech stocks take brunt of fears
articles.excerpt: Mainland and Hong Kong stocks ended sharply lower on Friday, with tech shares leading losses after a steep Wall Street…
articles.fullText:
Mainland and Hong Kong stocks ended sharply lower on Friday, with tech shares leading losses after a steep Wall Street selloff weighed on investor sentiment, while Anthropic's much-anticipated IPO did little to revive waning optimism surrounding the artificial intelligence sector.

The benchmark Hang Seng Index ended 430 points, or 1.9 percent, lower at 22,410 on turnover of HK$270.3 billion.

The tech index dived 138 points, or 3.8 percent, to 3,511 while the China enterprises index was 135 points, or 1.8 percent, down at 7,554.

Up north, the Shanghai Composite Index closed down 43 points, or 1.22 percent, at 3,533 on turnover of 702.57 billion yuan while the blue-chip CSI300 index lost 0.8 percent.

Both indexes recorded their lowest closing levels since July 2025.

For the week, the Shanghai Composite fell 2.8 percent to notch the biggest weekly drop since July, and the CSI300 lost 1.5 percent.

Investor sentiment was also weighed down by signs that Washington is tightening tech curbs on China, despite meetings between the leaders of the world's two largest economies this week.

The Shenzhen Component Index closed down 326 points, or 3.09 percent, at 10,256 on turnover of 719.62 billion yuan while the ChiNext Index closed down 81 points, or 3.54 percent, at 2,212 on turnover of 334.97 billion yuan.

The decline came after US stocks slumped on Thursday, as AI-related shares came under pressure following Anthropic's much-anticipated IPO's failure to sustain an early rally.

"The optimism failed to lift the broader AI sector, as concerns over stretched valuations and elevated capex spending continued to weigh on sentiment," analysts at OCBC said in a note.

In China, tech sectors that require huge computing power, such as big data, AI and cloud computing all fell sharply.

Hong Kong-listed shares of Chinese AI model developers, which rely heavily on advanced computing power, also tumbled.

Minimax slumped 10.8 percent to record lows, bringing this week's loss to more than 30 percent.

Z.AI shares declined 7.2 percent, bringing the weekly loss to 18.2 percent.

Semiconductor shares were among the biggest drags, with a subindex tracking the sector plunging 3.9 percent.

Sentiment towards chipmakers was also hurt by TSMC tightening restrictions on Chinese chip designers, suspending some previously permitted advanced manufacturing orders and generally limiting affected customers to older chipmaking technology, sources said.

In Tokyo, the Nikkei ended 3,007 points, or 5.06 percent, at 56,436 amid chip and tech related plunges of 10.32 percent for Advantest, 7.06 percent for Tokyo Electron, 14.48 percent for technology investor SoftBank Group and 11.66 percent for memory chip maker Kioxia.

For the week, the index lost 7.7 percent.

The broader Topix fell 148 points, or 3.88 percent, to 3,674 for the day.

In Seoul, the Kospi closed down 267 points, or 5.21 percent, at 4,869 as chipmaker losses of 7.01 percent piled up for Samsung Electronics and 5.92 percent for SK Hynix. (Agencies)

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: Beijing warns of 'judicial overreach' in ICJ ruling
articles.excerpt: China raised concerns of judicial overreach after the International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against its…
articles.fullText:
China raised concerns of judicial overreach after the International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, saying on Friday "such practices are not conducive" to a resolution.

"China is concerned about issues such as jurisdiction overreach and expanded interpretation, and believes that such practices are not conducive to the settlement of disputes," Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said when asked about the ICJ ruling.

"The international community should make joint efforts in this direction to avoid complicating this issue," he added.

Guo was speaking as Malaysia said it would resettle 10,000 Rohingya refugees in Turkiye through a structured skills training programme, in what would be one of the biggest resettlement initiatives involving the Rohingya.

The proposal is part of the government's efforts to address the Rohingya refugee situation in Malaysia in a more "coordinated, effective and humane manner", Malaysian Deputy Prime Minister Ahmad Zahid Hamidi said in a statement.

"I welcome the government of Turkiye's agreement to receive 10,000 Rohingya refugees. This marks an important step in Malaysia's efforts to find a long-term solution to an issue that has long posed challenges for migration management and national security," he said.

Ahmad Zahid said the initiative with Turkey could serve as a model for how countries can work together to manage refugee resettlement. (AFP/Reuters)

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: Stiffer penalties in works in Buildings Ordinance fix
articles.excerpt: The government is proposing to tighten the Buildings Ordinance and raise maximum penalties to HK$10 million and five years in…
articles.fullText:
The government is proposing to tighten the Buildings Ordinance and raise maximum penalties to HK$10 million and five years in prison for all works, including those involving large-scale maintenance, that cause death, injury or property damage.

The proposals come in the wake of the Wang Fuk Court fire last November.

In a paper submitted to Legco, the Development Bureau proposed creating a new, separately regulated category for large-scale building maintenance works that no longer treats them as low-risk minor repairs.

A project qualifies as large-scale maintenance if the building involved is four storeys or above and the scaffolding covers one whole side of the building, across at least four floors.

These works, which currently only need to be notified, would require a Buildings Department permit before they could start – and an authorised person would have to submit prescribed plans and a supervision plan.

Inspection and supervisory duties would be split, and the authorised person would have to declare that there is no conflict of interest with the inspection consultant and the contractor.

All materials used in construction – such as concrete, fire doors, scaffolding materials and temporary window coverings – must meet standards set by the Building Department.

Use of substandard materials would carry a fine of up to HK$3 million and three years' imprisonment, against HK$500,000 and 18 months under present minor-works rules.

Work carried out in a way that causes or may cause death, injury or property damage would come under a new criminal offence that carries a fine of up to HK$10 million and five years’ imprisonment, against HK$1 million and three years at present.

A finding of bribery or bid-rigging could result in one being struck off statutory contractor and consultant registers without a disciplinary hearing and being banned for three years.

The government aims to introduce the amendment bill in January and bring it into force by the middle of 2027.

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: HK 'can blossom amid growth in regionalism'
articles.excerpt: China experts on Friday urged Hong Kong to carve out a new economic strategy and lean into regional growth while…
articles.fullText:
China experts on Friday urged Hong Kong to carve out a new economic strategy and lean into regional growth while warning that global energy policies remained at odds with climate goals.

Their comments came a day after the Apec summit wrapped up in Shenzhen, where talks and discussions centred on Asia-Pacific trade and economic cooperation, technology and innovation, and major-power diplomacy.

Speaking on RTHK's Backchat programme on Friday, Einar Tangen, a senior fellow at the Centre for International Governance Innovation, said global trade was shifting towards regional blocs and that Hong Kong and the Greater Bay Area had a strategic role to play within Asia.

“The world is dividing, and you can quite clearly see the growth of regionalism and this is what Apec was about, and then you have entities within that sphere like Hong Kong and Greater Bay Area, which are there to serve it,” he said.

“It doesn't mean that they will not have robust interactions with Europe and America and etc, but they form a vital function in an emerging economy where China and Asean are now beyond one trillion dollars.”

Tangen also noted that it’s time to start re-evaluating and seeing the Global South more as a primary focus for development opportunities, where Hong Kong and Shenzhen are going to blossom and serve the region.

For his part, Victor Gao, vice president of the Centre for China and Globalisation, suggested the city come up with a new strategy for ways to deal with upcoming challenges and opportunities.

The relative advantages that Hong Kong has enjoyed for many years ago now is fast dwindling, he said, and it should learn from the great example of places such as Shenzhen and always be committed to pushing forward to scale real heights.

Gao emphasised that complacency, inefficiency or a failure to reach new heights will likely hinder Hong Kong’s prospects for major economic and financial achievements in the coming years.

Josef Gregory Mahoney, professor of politics and international relations at East China Normal University, gave his take on the outcome of the trilateral summit involving China, the United States and Russia at the Apec summit.

He noted that while China was working to accelerate green transformation and reduce global carbon emissions, both the US and Russia remained heavily reliant on fossil fuels.

“The thing that concerns me most about the declaration is that you have two fossil fuel-dependent economies, Russia and the United States, and you have China, which is trying to accelerate green transformations and make the world less dependent on climate change-causing energy carbon emissions,” Mahoney said.

He also pointed out that the ongoing global energy shock stemmed from the conflict with Ukraine as well as US actions involving Venezuela and Iran, saying a resolution to increase oil production runs counter to broader climate goals.

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: PNG has the legal right to close down Taiwan’s office, but at what cost?
articles.excerpt: After Taiwan pulls out of Port Moresby, analysts weigh the pros and cons of closer ties with China.
articles.fullText:
PORT MORESBY, Papua New Guinea – The decision by Papua New Guinea to order Taiwan’s representative office in Port Moresby to close is well within the country’s legal rights, but the legal and geopolitical considerations for such a decision are distinct, a commercial lawyer based in the South Pacific country told Radio Free Asia.
In July , PNG’s Foreign Affairs Minister Justin Tkatchenko announced in an official statement the immediate cessation of operations and the formal closure of the physical presence of the Chinese Taipei Economic Office, citing Port Moresby’s recognition of Beijing.
The office served as Taiwan’s de facto diplomatic mission in PNG, facilitating trade and other exchanges despite the absence of formal diplomatic relations between the two sides.
Taiwan on Nov. 6 confirmed the office would shut down, its personnel would withdraw, and all technical missions, scholarship and training programs would cease. Taipei also announced that it would stop spot purchases of PNG’s liquefied natural gas, or LNG, Port Moresby’s largest export commodity. Prior to the closure, Taiwan had purchased about a third of PNG’s LNG exports.
The decision to force Taiwan to close its representative office is less a legal matter than a policy decision, Margareth Parua, a Port Moresby-based commercial lawyer, told RFA.
“On the information presently available, there is no clearly identified international legal obligation requiring PNG to close an unofficial Taiwanese trade office merely because it recognises the People’s Republic of China,” she said. “Given the longstanding economic and commercial relationship between PNG and Taiwan, it would be regrettable if the decision resulted in the unnecessary loss of trade, investment and other opportunities for our people.”
Weighing options
One year after PNG gained its independence from Australia in 1975, it recognized Beijing diplomatically, adopting its own version of a “One-China Policy” which closely aligns with Beijing’s “One-China Principle” that there is only one China, Taiwan is a part of China, and that the government in Beijing is the sole legal government of China. This differs from the One China Policy of the United States in that Washington’s policy merely acknowledges Beijing’s stance on Taiwan without agreeing or disagreeing with it.
Neither Port Moresby’s One-China Policy precluded unofficial relations with Taiwan, but Beijing has recently leveraged its economic might to pressure Pacific island countries in an effort to further isolate Taiwan, Jonah Bock, assistant director for research at the Alliance Futures Initiative, a Washington-based think tank, told RFA shortly after Tkatchenko’s announcement in July.
“China will continue to aggressively pursue any action that reduces Taiwan’s international space – its ethos of national rejuvenation relies on unification. It is not an option for China to stop the contest,” said Bock in July. “The move is to curry favor with the PRC and the goal is vast sums of Chinese money.”
China's President Xi Jinping (R) shakes hands with Papua New Guinea's Prime Minister James Marape before leaders take a group photo during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit in Shenzhen, in China's southern Guangdong Province, on Nov. 19, 2026.
(Greg Baker/Pool via Reuters) Parua said that PNG should carefully consider whether forcing Taipei to close its representative office was necessary to maintain its One-China Policy, and whether the benefits of doing so outweigh the costs to national interest.
The biggest risk might have been the loss of LNG sales to Taiwan, but closer ties with China can make up for that, Joseph Ealedona, a Papua New Guinean senior journalist and former media executive, told RFA.
“While we lost the gas sales, discussions are taking place for China to purchase more gas to cover for this,” he said. “It’s a positive decision given our deep relations with China and the many benefits we can take from China. China is a massive economy and we must maintain our relations with them.”
Meanwhile, PNG’s former Prime Minister Peter O’Neill commented in Port Moresby-based weekly English daily The National that the country had lost a major buyer in Taiwan, and criticized current Prime Minister James Marape saying he traded Taiwan for China and 191 million kina (US$42.2 million).
Taipei disappointed, Washington concerned, but Beijing jubilant
Taiwan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs expressed regret in its official statement on Nov. 6 announcing the closure of the representative office. The statement detailed how Taiwan had given Papua New Guinea economic, agricultural, developmental and medical support over the years.
“Regrettably, the foundation of mutual trust, established through long-term bilateral collaboration, has been seriously undermined by the recent actions of the government of Papua New Guinea,” the statement said. “The situation also reflects China’s continued use of political pressure and economic influence to interfere in the diplomatic decisions of other nations and suppress Taiwan’s international participation.”
The statement also said that the change would have a “substantial impact” on PNG’s natural gas exports.
A man walks in front of flags of Honduras, Taiwan, and other countries, displayed at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs building, in Taipei, Taiwan on March 23, 2023.
(Annabelle Chih/Reuters) A U.S. State Department spokesperson told RFA on Nov. 9 that Washington was “deeply concerned” that PNG had ordered Taipei’s office in Port Moresby closed.
“Taiwan is a reliable, likeminded, and democratic partner, and its relationships around the world provide significant benefits to the citizens of those countries, including Papua New Guinea,” the spokesperson said. “This is yet another example of Beijing’s intimidation campaign against Taiwan and its supporters around the world, which undermines the sovereign decisions of countries choosing to partner with Taiwan and threatens international peace and prosperity.”
The Chinese Embassy in Port Moresby on Nov. 10 said in a statement that the PNG government made the right decision, and criticized Taiwan’s statement as being full of “lies and empty threats.”
“We highly appreciate and applaud the PNG Government’s firm adherence to one-China principle and the concrete measures to implement this principle, which will further consolidate the political foundation for China-PNG bilateral relations and cooperation in various fields,” the statement said. “If the Taiwan side reduces its LNG imports from PNG, the loss will on its side instead of PNG side.”
Beijing also said spot purchases of PNG’s LNG would find new buyers, including China.
“As to Taiwan’s ‘assistance’ to PNG, it is almost nothing compared to the aid and assistance from China’s mainland.”
Additional reporting by Eugene Whong in Washington. Edited by Taejun Kang and Eugene Whong.

articles.title: 'China, Australia should be mutually trusted partners'
articles.excerpt: President Xi Jinping said on Friday that China and Australia should be cooperative partners who trust each other and help…
articles.fullText:
President Xi Jinping said on Friday that China and Australia should be cooperative partners who trust each other and help each other succeed, as the two countries have no historical grievances or fundamental conflicts of interests.

China-Australia relations are stable at present, he said when meeting Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese in Shenzhen.

Xi said that in a volatile and turbulent world, the two countries should enhance mutual trust, accommodate each other's core interests and major concerns, and keep to the right direction of friendship and cooperation.

China and Australia have brought about a comprehensive turnaround in bilateral relations, he said.

Xi called for deepening mutually beneficial cooperation in pursuit of the two countries' respective development goals, advancing traditional cooperation in agriculture, energy and minerals, and expanding cooperation in emerging areas such as the green economy, new energy, the digital industry, artificial intelligence and climate change response.

Efforts should be made to promote friendship between the two countries through expanded people-to-people exchanges, Xi said, noting that the two sides had agreed to designate 2027 as the China-Australia Year of Tourism.

For his part, Albanese said Australia and China share an interest in open and rules-based trade.

"The relationship that we are building is positive, is calm, is not defined by our differences, but one where we can have clear and frank exchanges for our mutual interest," he said.

The meeting with Albanese came as Xi pursued a packed schedule of bilateral meetings with foreign leaders in the aftermath of the Apec Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen.

Other leaders whom he met on Friday included prime ministers Lawrence Wong of Singapore, Anwar Ibrahim of Malaysia and Anutin Charnvirakul of Thailand as well as President Prabowo Subianto of Indonesia.

Wong congratulated Xi on his historic trilateral summit with Russia and the United States and said he was "looking to build on government-to-government initiatives to deepen our economic ties further", referring to projects in Suzhou, Tianjin and Chongqing.

In the meeting between Xi and Prabowo, the leaders announced the launch of negotiations for a bilateral comprehensive economic partnership.

Xi said China and Indonesia should strengthen strategic communication and solidarity, deepen all-round strategic cooperation, consolidate the foundation of political trust, and jointly guard against and respond to external risks.

He called on both countries to expand mutually beneficial cooperation, advance major projects such as the Jakarta-Bandung High-Speed Railway, and deepen cooperation in energy and mineral resources, artificial intelligence, the digital economy, and clean energy. (Xinhua & Reuters)

Edited by Altis Wong

articles.title: Building maintenance body to get over HK$400mn
articles.excerpt: The government said on Friday that more money will be allocated to subsidise owners of older buildings to pay for…
articles.fullText:
The government said on Friday that more money will be allocated to subsidise owners of older buildings to pay for a new one-stop maintenance service to help owners prepare tenders, evaluate bids and monitor construction works.

In a paper submitted to Legco, the Development Bureau says it plans to transfer the remaining balance of about HK$113 million from the Urban Renewal Authority's Smart Tender scheme into the new Building Maintenance Support and Services Council to be set up by the end of the year.

Together with the HK$300 million reserved by the government, the total comes to about HK$413 million.

The new council is being set up following the independent committee's report into the Wang Fuk Court fire, which found serious failures in building maintenance oversight.

Of the total, HK$313 million will be used to subsidise owners to use a paid service provided by the council to appoint consultants and contractors that it recommends. The standard fee is initially estimated at several thousand dollars per household, with details to be announced later.

"We believe that the reformed service arrangements can effectively reduce the risk of bid-rigging and provide owners with end-to-end, more effective and practical assistance in carrying out building maintenance works," it says.

The government says the subsidy will target owners of older buildings with lower rateable values – covering 80 percent of private residential and composite buildings aged 30 or above.

Authorities recommend that the remaining 20 percent, which have relatively high property prices, would have to pay for such services in full.

Edited by Cecil Wong

articles.title: HK joins global drug regulatory body ICH
articles.excerpt: Hong Kong has formally become a regulatory member of the International Council for Harmonisation of Technical Requirements for Pharmaceuticals for…
articles.fullText:
Hong Kong has formally become a regulatory member of the International Council for Harmonisation of Technical Requirements for Pharmaceuticals for Human Use (ICH), a move the Health Bureau says marks a key step towards building the city into an international healthcare innovation hub.

The ICH admitted Hong Kong, represented by the Pharmacy and Poisons Board, as its 20th regulatory member at its assembly in the Czech Republic on Tuesday.

Other regulatory members include the National Medical Products Administration of China, as well as regulators from Europe, Switzerland, the UK and the US.

The ICH is a key international platform for coordinating technical standards on drug regulation, setting guidelines covering safety, efficacy and quality.

Secretary for Health Lo Chung-mau said the government sincerely thanked the country for its support for Hong Kong's development as an international healthcare innovation hub, saying the membership fully demonstrates the unique advantages of "one country, two systems".

He noted that Hong Kong became an ICH observer on October 31, 2023, and had met all of the body's requirements in just three years, far faster than the eight to 10 years estimated earlier.

Lo said the government will set up a centre for medical products regulation to build independent drug evaluation and approval capacity to support clinical research on biopharmaceuticals.

"The HKSAR Government will establish the Centre for Medical Products Regulation (CMPR) next month to build up capacity for independent drug evaluation and approval, and actively participate in international co-operation, with a view to developing Hong Kong into an international health and medical innovation hub and better integrating into and serving the overall national development," he said.

Director of Health Ronald Lam said joining the ICH is a big step forward.

"This is actually an important milestone in the development of drug and medical device regulation in Hong Kong, and it also marks the most critical step forward in establishing an internationally recognised, independent drug evaluation authority," Lam said.

Lam said the soon-to-be-established centre will build a professional team in accordance with ICH technical requirements, send experts to take part in drafting and revising ICH guidelines, and strive to become an internationally authoritative regulator.

Edited by Cecil Wong

articles.title: 'Apec leaders have will to tackle uncertainty'
articles.excerpt: There is a strong political will among Apec members to work together to address the region's challenges despite geopolitical tensions…
articles.fullText:
There is a strong political will among Apec members to work together to address the region's challenges despite geopolitical tensions and rapid technological change, and Apec leaders believe these issues can be tackled collectively, Apec Secretariat chief Eduardo Pedrosa said in Hong Kong on Friday.

Speaking at a young entrepreneur summit, Pedrosa said the collective will among members was one of the clearest messages he took away from the leaders' meeting that concluded in Shenzhen on Thursday.

"Given all of the tensions that we face, disagreements that we have, there is a very strong political will to address this uncertainty. And this is, I think, going to be critical as we try to nurture the next generation of entrepreneurs," he said.

He noted that 97 per cent of businesses across Apec economies are micro, or small and medium-sized enterprises, and that the future of the region's economies depends on such firms.

"The future of our economies depends on businesses like yours reaching their full potential," he said.

Pedrosa said the policies Apec recommends are ultimately there to create value, innovation and jobs, and that its work is about applying technology to solve everyday problems rather than change for its own sake.

He said Apec is a policy-oriented organisation that facilitates dialogue among officials, while also building networks of government workers, academics and business people who put its recommendations into practice.

He noted that about 200,000 new companies are registered in Hong Kong each year, and urged young entrepreneurs to engage with Apec as they grow their businesses.

He also shared what he called a lesson from a token bag he was given in Shenzhen while attending the Apec meetings, which read: "When you want to make an elevator pitch, take the stairs." He said he took it to mean entrepreneurs should take their time, step back and think deeply – adding that taking risks and trying new ideas matters, even when some ideas fail.

Edited by Cecil Wong

articles.title: New levy set to fund free EV battery recycling
articles.excerpt: The government is proposing a producer responsibility scheme that will give electric vehicle owners a one-off free battery recycling service…
articles.fullText:
The government is proposing a producer responsibility scheme that will give electric vehicle owners a one-off free battery recycling service – with carmakers paying an upfront levy to the Environmental Protection Department before distributing new vehicles or batteries.

The scheme is aimed at stopping EV batteries from being improperly thrown away – and to boost recycling.

In a paper submitted to the Legislative Council, the government says there are currently 180,000 EVs on the road.

Retired batteries are expected to weigh in at around 6,700 tonnes in 2030, up from about 1,300 tonnes this year.

EV batteries typically last five to 10 years – meaning there is a long gap between when they enter the market and when they are eventually retired, it says.

"During this period, the original suppliers of batteries may have closed their businesses or exited the Hong Kong market, or it may be difficult to track the whereabouts of individual vehicles and batteries," the government said.

"The trade considers it necessary to impose a levy at source when batteries are introduced into the market to ensure the availability of stable and sufficient financial resources for supporting the proper recycling of retired batteries in the future."

To enable the market to adapt gradually, the government proposes setting the levy at a relatively low initial rate, that is HK$6 per kilogramme, followed by steady annual increments.

For a typical car with a 500-kilogramme battery, the initial charge in 2028 would be about HK$3,000, rising by HK$800 a year to HK$15,000 by 2043.

When replacing a battery or scrapping a vehicle, owners would take it to a designated return point, or hand it over through a workshop or scrapyard, and must complete and sign a declaration.

An application to the Transport Department to cancel a vehicle’s registration would also be treated as meeting that requirement.

The levy would be waived for electric vehicles already on the road, but those owners would still get the free recycling and scrapping service.

The government aims to submit the bill in 2027 and the scheme is expected to be fully implemented in 2029.

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: HK can make contribution to construction sector: CE
articles.excerpt: Hong Kong is well placed to contribute to the national effort to enhance the construction sector's global standing and competitiveness…
articles.fullText:
Hong Kong is well placed to contribute to the national effort to enhance the construction sector's global standing and competitiveness, Chief Executive John Lee said.

Lee said the national 15th Five-Year Plan calls for raising the construction sector's global standing, and that Hong Kong connects the country's capabilities with international opportunities while providing professional support to turn them into successful projects.

"In a world shaped by shifting geopolitics, urgent climate challenges, and rapid technological advance, insights alone are not enough. We must turn ideas into projects with lasting impact," he said at the opening ceremony of the inaugural InfraEX Week, which brings together some 800 infrastructure project leaders, government officials and professionals from over 30 countries and economies.

Lee said the SAR's first five-year plan, closely aligned with the national version, offers a strategic roadmap for the city's future while enabling Hong Kong to better integrate into and serve the overall national development.

A clear example, he said, is the Northern Metropolis, which takes up a third of Hong Kong's geographical area and will eventually be home to some 2.5 million people, create half a million jobs and account for about 13 percent of the city's GDP.

He said the Hong Kong Park of the Hetao Shenzhen-Hong Kong Science and Technology Innovation Cooperation Zone and three planned university towns would integrate innovation, industry and education.

Lee said the city must deliver projects that are truly future-ready, and that means "quality, more than quantity."

"To build the Northern Metropolis and all that it promises, we must deliver infrastructure that is truly future-ready, and that means quality more than quantity."

He said artificial intelligence, advanced engineering technologies, construction robots and digital supervision systems are being deployed to improve productivity and cost-effectiveness.

Lee also highlighted the city's services expertise, spanning engineering, project management, legal and financial services, and cited a footbridge built with home-produced S960 high-strength steel as an example of Hong Kong's role as a super connector and super value-adder, bridging standards and validating innovation.

He added that collaboration would take concrete shape with the exchange of memorandums of understanding and a letter of intent with international and local partners.

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: HK stocks slip as Anthropic IPO fails to end AI slump
articles.excerpt: Asian shares slid on Friday to be on track for their worst week since 2020 as Anthropic's debut failed to…
articles.fullText:
