This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.

A human liver has been kept alive outside the body for a record seven weeks

Researchers in Australia claim they’ve kept a human liver alive on life support outside the body for seven weeks, smashing the previous record of about two weeks.

They achieved the feat by connecting a donated liver to a system of automated pumps and sensors that fed the organ nutrients, supplied it with blood, and whisked away waste.

The approach could open up new possibilities in biomedical engineering, from repairing damaged organs to growing new ones. Some researchers are even exploring artificial wombs.

Take a closer look at the technology keeping human organs alive .

—Antonio Regalado

What a billion-dollar deal says about the US battery market

After a tough few years littered with high-profile failures, there’s some positive news for next-generation batteries in the US: Sila has signed a deal with battery maker Panasonic Energy to supply silicon-carbon anode material that could be worth more than $1 billion.

The agreement will help Sila scale production, potentially bringing smaller, lighter batteries to market. But it also reveals how battery politics have shifted. The factory is backed by a $1.4 billion loan from the Trump administration’s Defense Department—and the industry is increasingly focused on geopolitics rather than the energy transition.

Find out what this deal reveals about the US battery industry .

—Casey Crownhart

This story is from The Spark, our weekly climate tech newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Wednesday.

The AI Hype Index returns

Separating AI reality from hyped-up fiction isn’t always easy. That’s why we’ve created the AI Hype Index—a simple, at-a-glance summary of what’s shaping the industry right now.

The latest edition tracks AI’s spread across everything from literary prizes and cyberattacks to a Grok-ified version of The Odyssey . See where it all landed on this month’s index .

The must-reads

I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.

1 Anthropic has raised $81 billion in the biggest-ever IPO
It eclipsed SpaceX as the largest stock-market debut. ( Bloomberg $)
+ Its stated mission could conflict with shareholders’ interests. ( NYT $)
+ The IPO comes amid new safety fears about its AI advances. ( FT $)
+ Its performance will test the strength of the AI boom. ( BBC )
+ What even is the AI bubble? ( MIT Technology Review )

2 China is reportedly seeking Nvidia chips for AI-powered weapons
Beijing is trying to circumvent US export controls. ( CNBC )
+ Alibaba tapped Nvidia to support a military-linked lab. ( NYT $)
+ When the US military implemented AI, civilian deaths rose . ( Intercept )
+ “Humans in the loop” in AI war is an illusion. ( MIT Technology Review )

3 Elon Musk has joined Silicon Valley’s retreat from Trump
He called his midterm spending “foolish” and broke with MAGA. ( FT $)
+ OpenAI and Palantir leaders have also struck new tones. ( Gizmodo )
+ Silicon Valley got the midterms badly wrong. ( MIT Technology Review )

4 Ukraine used relay drones to strike Putin’s bridge without Starlink
The strike showed how it’s learning to fight without SpaceX. ( Ars Technica )
+ Musk has denied Kyiv’s claims about restrictions on Starlink. ( CNBC )

5 A major cyberattack has hit the European Commission
It may have exposed large amounts of staff personal data. ( Politico )
+ Trump has blamed Minnesota for water system hacks. ( ABC )

6 Trump may force US firms to disclose their use of Chinese AI
The proposal aims to discourage reliance on Chinese models. ( Reuters $)

7 The US has slashed funding for biomedical science abroad
It’s also weakened oversight of foreign grants. ( Economist $)

The US and China are turning to fossil fuels to power AI. ( Guardian )
+ The climate case for AI has not been made. ( MIT Technology Review )

It scored 99 out of 100 on review aggregation site Metacritic. ( BBC )
+ Schools and businesses are bracing for “GTA Flu” season. ( NYT $)

Aquanauts there will monitor struggling ecosystems. ( New Scientist $)

Quote of the day

“Here are some of the smartest people on the planet being completely idiotic.”

—Thomas Nagel, a philosopher and professor emeritus at NYU, tells Wired why he objects to Anthropic giving Claude more independence, just as the company makes its record-breaking stock-market debut.

One more thing

China has approved the world’s first invasive brain-computer chip—here’s what’s next

Sitting in the courtyard of his house in China’s Henan province last October, Dong Hui decided to try holding a pen. Six years after a car accident left him paralyzed from the neck down, he slowly wrote his name, “Thank you,” and the date.

The breakthrough was made possible by a brain implant called NEO. In March, it became the world’s first invasive brain-computer interface approved for use beyond clinical trials. The approval is expected to accelerate China’s push to become a global leader in brain implants.

Here’s how China reached the milestone—and what it means for the future of BCIs .

—You Xiaoying

We can still have nice things

A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line .)

articles.title: A human liver has been kept alive outside the body for a record seven weeks
articles.excerpt: Researchers in Australia claim they’ve kept a human liver alive, on life support, outside the body for seven weeks, opening…
articles.fullText:
Researchers in Australia claim they’ve kept a human liver alive, on life support, outside the body for seven weeks, opening up speculative new possibilities in biomedical engineering.

The feat, whose details are pending publication, was carried out in Sydney after a team led by surgeon and inventor Carlo Pulitano connected a donated liver to a system of automated pumps and sensors that fed the organ nutrients, supplied it with blood, and whisked away waste.

In an interview, Pulitano, a transplant surgeon at the Royal Prince Alfred Hospital and a professor at the University of Sydney, likened the life support system to “an artificial body.” Its official name is the Extended Organ Perfusion System.

“Our group is the only one in the world to have maintained a human liver under fully normothermic, physiological conditions for seven weeks,” he says.

Normothermic means body temperature, or about 37 °C. The previous record for keeping an internal organ alive outside the body was set in Switzerland several years ago. That organ—also a liver—lasted around two weeks.

Most organs destined for transplant survive only a few hours in special ice buckets and need to be raced to their destination. Over the last decade, however, surgeons have been switching to perfusion systems, which pump warm or cold fluids into an organ. This can double the time it can be held before it must be transplanted.

Pulitano says the key to breaking the record was to automate the systems used to keep the organ thriving. During a meeting in Switzerland earlier this year, the Sydney team described perfusing 55 human livers, one after the other. Some were connected to a system that needed to be adjusted manually, but for those placed on the automated system—which produced the seven-week survivor—the average survival time tripled, to about four weeks.

Perfusion has already enabled doctors to restart hearts from dead people and keep them beating outside the body. Paulo Martins, a transplant doctor at the University of Oklahoma, says about half the kidneys he transplants are now perfused, even though the process can add $100,000 to the cost of a transplant.

While the research awaits formal publication, the eventual goal is what Pulitano and colleagues call “time-unlimited liver preservation.”

Scientists have already discovered possible medical benefits to keeping organs on life support longer than usual. One, they say, is that perfused organs apparently start to repair themselves and become stronger after a day or so. That’s what led a Swiss team, in 2022, to transplant a damaged liver that had been kept on perfusion for three days —the longest time any internal organ had remained outside the body before a successful transplant, says Waldemar Hoffmann, the CEO and cofounder of Apersys, a startup formed to commercialize the technology.

Pulitano says his own startup, Aeternum Life Technologies, will be helping with a planned trial in Sydney to transplant low-quality livers kept on perfusion for four days.

What’s less clear, says Hoffmann, is whether any transplant surgeon would ever want, or need, to use an organ kept alive for nearly two months. He says people in the field believe Pulitano’s record is real, but they don’t know how healthy the organ was at the end or even what so much extra time is likely to achieve. “The key question is what the purpose for a seven-week perfusion would be,” he says.

Yet that’s where things could start to get interesting, says Martins , the Oklahoma surgeon. Long-term life support could enable far-out concepts like artificial wombs, new types of organ manufacturing, and the chance to experiment directly on human organs outside the body for extended periods.

For his part, Pulitano says long-term machine perfusion could help grow new organs. In living donations, surgeons commonly take half of a person’s liver to give someone else. After about two months, both parts will have grown back almost to their full volume. Pulitano says he’s tried dividing a liver and then attaching the sections to the machine. If that works, he says, it could be a way to multiply one donor liver into several full-size organs.

“It’s important to have people thinking outside the box and pushing the limits and creating possibilities for things that, right now, sometimes we don’t even have a need for but are going to be needed in the future,” says Martins. “That’s how science moves.”

He’s not the only one who thinks so. For instance, a US company, Bexorg, has been reanimating human brains using perfusion pumps. The idea is to study what effects experimental drugs have on them. That company perfuses brains for about a day but has said it wants to extend the time to two weeks.

Similar experiments can be done on livers, says Pulitano, who has already tried adding gene therapies to the organs. “It gives us a living human organ model for translational research that no animal system can match, because the biology, the immunology, and the drug responses are human from the outset,” he says.

Meanwhile, in Silicon Valley, patents filed by Altos Labs , a billionaire-backed longevity startup, describe attempts to introduce reprogramming genes into animal livers maintained outside the body. Eventually, Altos scientists have speculated, they might temporarily disconnect a failing organ while it’s still in a person’s body, connecting it to a perfusion machine in order to douse it with ultra-powerful genetic treatments without risking the rest of the body.

Doctors probing the limits of organ life support have now formed two new scientific societies to explore the concept. One, founded by Martins and called the International Society for Organ Preservation and Perfusion Therapy, will hold its inaugural meeting this year in Italy. The other, based in China, was launched in August to advance what doctors at the First Affiliated Hospital of Sun Yat-Sen University have termed “ organ medicine” : research at the level of whole organs kept alive by “bionic maintenance.”

“What is exploding is the idea of this technology that clearly goes beyond simply organ preservation,” says Pulitano. “Basically, that’s a concept that’s entirely new.”

articles.title: What a billion-dollar deal says about the US battery market
articles.excerpt: After a tough few years littered with some high-profile failures, there’s some positive news for next-generation batteries in the US…
articles.fullText:
After a tough few years littered with some high-profile failures, there’s some positive news for next-generation batteries in the US.

Sila just signed an agreement with Panasonic Energy, a global battery manufacturer, to supply silicon-carbon anode material, a possible key to smaller, lighter batteries. It’s a deal that Sila says could be worth more than $1 billion over time.

This arrangement also shows how much the politics of batteries have shifted lately. A major part of the financial backing for this factory’s production is a $1.4 billion loan from the Trump administration’s Defense Department. While batteries can be a major tool to help drive the energy transition and cut emissions, right now much of the industry is more focused on geopolitics.

Founded in 2011, Sila makes silicon-based anodes for lithium-ion batteries. The big selling point here is the potential to improve energy density—Sila’s anode weighs a fifth as much as the graphite used in anodes today and cuts the volume in half, according to the company. So using this new material enables batteries to pack more energy into the same weight and volume, allowing longer range for EVs, for example. The material can also deliver more power and recharge faster, compared with conventional chemistry.

We’ve been following Sila (and its competitors) for years. My colleague James Temple covered the company when its battery first appeared in Whoop fitness wearables in 2021.

Things have gotten a lot bigger since then. In 2022, Sila announced plans for a factory in Moses Lake, Washington, and received $100 million from the US Department of Energy, part of a multibillion-dollar round of grants under the Biden administration to support the US battery supply chain.

The company opened its factory in September 2025, and it’s already operating. But the deal with Panasonic will help it scale to at least 10 times more production than current levels, says Gene Berdichevsky, the company’s cofounder and CEO.

Panasonic has committed to buying tens of thousands of tons of material, Berdichevsky says, though Sila isn’t sharing specific numbers on the total commitment or the price Panasonic is paying.

This agreement is Sila’s first mass-market deal and a big one for the United States’ next-generation battery market, which has largely been on the ropes over the past few years. Two billion-dollar battery companies, 24M and ESS Tech , have declared bankruptcy and shut down just in the last year.

The glimmer of hope here is tied up with something I’ve been noticing about this industry: the shifting politics. While batteries used to be firmly considered a climate technology, we’ve seen a lot of companies move away from messaging around the clean energy transition and lean into geopolitics.

China dominates the battery world and particularly the battery anode market, controlling over 90% of graphite production today. For years, the US has been trying to curb reliance on Chinese batteries, battery materials, and other materials used in crucial technologies, like rare earth metals. But the Trump administration has ramped things up, and earlier this year the US Defense Department committed a $1.4 billion loan to Sila aimed at helping the US face a “significant technology sovereignty challenge,” as a press release put it.

Sila’s announcement of the Panasonic deal does mention EVs—but not climate, emissions or the energy transition. Rather, it’s all about American industrialization. (And, of course, a mention that a North American battery supply chain can also help power the AI market.)

I asked Berdichevsky about this shift and whether the company holds decarbonization as a priority.

“I think the politics of it has shifted around us much more than our motivations have shifted,” he said. “It’s really the energy efficiency that motivates engineers like myself and technologists at our company. And I still think that that’s still at the heart of it.”

This article is from The Spark, MIT Technology Review ’s weekly climate newsletter. To receive it in your inbox every Wednesday, sign up here .

articles.title: HK, Singapore leaders meet on Apec sidelines

The leaders of Hong Kong and Singapore on Thursday discussed fostering closer ties on the sidelines of the Apec summit.

Chief Executive John Lee said in his meeting with Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong that they discussed Hong Kong’s first five-year plan.

“I’m thankful because it just strengthened our partnership and relationship,” Lee said.

Wong, for his part, said exchanges between the two governments have continued at various levels, such as the Singapore-Hong Kong Permanent Secretaries Exchange Programme which was held in Singapore in July.

“The ties are warmer than ever, and I look forward to building even closer cooperation between our two cities,” he said.

Lee agreed that the exchange programme was working very well and suggested that next year’s exchange take place in Hong Kong.

In his social media post, Lee thanked Singapore for its continued support for the SAR’s early accession to Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP), as the Lion City takes up the Asean chairmanship next year.

“I welcome Singapore’s public and private sectors, including GIC and technology enterprises, to explore the business potential of the Hong Kong Park in the Hetao Co-operation Zone and deepen collaboration in areas such as artificial intelligence and biotechnology,” he wrote.

The CE said the two cities are both outward-oriented economies with strong track records in finance, trade and shipping.

He said commercial ties between the two cities are close, and that he looked forward to the further consolidation of their partnership.

Edited by Edmond Fong

"We intend to comprehensively advance our strategic and mutually beneficial relationship... pursuing dialogue to safeguard the national interests of both sides, and build a constructive and stable relationship," Takaichi said on the sidelines of the summit.

articles.title: HK, mainland stocks fall amid chip clampdown
articles.excerpt: Hong Kong's benchmark sank to four-month lows while mainland stocks remained under pressure, as fresh trade tensions flared up between…
articles.fullText:
Hong Kong's benchmark sank to four-month lows while mainland stocks remained under pressure, as fresh trade tensions flared up between China and the United States despite meetings between Presidents Xi Jinping and Donald Trump in Shenzhen.

The benchmark Hang Seng Index closed 453 points, or 1.9 percent, down at 22,841 on turnover of HK$229.55 billion.

The tech index fell 87 points, or 2.3 percent, to 3,649, hitting a 26-month low as it extended its losing streak to seven sessions, while the China enterprises index stumbled 145 points, or 1.9 percent, to 7,690.

Hong Kong-listed AI model developers and AI hyperscalers, whose competitiveness depends on advanced computing power, tumbled.

MiniMax slumped as much as 11 percent to record lows while Z.AI lost two percent.

Tencent tumbled nearly seven percent to a 31-month low after its third-quarter revenue missed forecasts, and the company said new US chip curbs may slow model training.

Alibaba tanked 5.5 percent to a 22-month low while Shanghai Iluvatar CoreX Semiconductor slumped 17 percent.

On the mainland, the Shanghai Composite Index fell 10 points, or 0.28 percent, to close at 3,577, its lowest level, in more than 15 months on turnover of 636.9 billion yuan.

The Shenzhen Component Index dropped 76 points, or 0.71 percent, to close at 10,583 on turnover of 668.23 billion yuan while the ChiNext Index declined 18 points, or 0.79 percent, to close at 2,293 on turnover of 310.12 billion yuan.

Tech stocks that rely on advanced chips, including cloud computing, AI and big data, led the declines

The losses came as Xi said on Thursday he remained committed to working with Trump to steer ties between their countries on the "correct course", even as the Commerce Ministry voiced strong opposition to a recent series of economic and trade restrictions the US imposed against China.

The Nvidia saga has led to tighter scrutiny of US chip exports to China.

The Trump administration is also considering requiring US companies to publicly disclose their use of Chinese AI models to discourage reliance on the technology.

Meanwhile, a US House panel asked Microsoft on Wednesday to brief lawmakers on a report that said the company could allow the Chinese firm ByteDance to use OpenAI models through Microsoft's Azure cloud platform.

These developments deepened investor worry that the world's two largest economies are careening towards a fresh tit-for-tat trade war, after the Republicans' defeat in the US midterms appears to have prompted the White House to take a more hawkish policy towards China.

In Tokyo, the Nikkei ended 419 points, or 0.71 percent, higher at 59,444, with Softbank Group gaining 4.5 percent and Advantest edging down 0.55 percent. The broader Topix edged down 0.04 percent to 3,822 in, like with the Nikkei, similarly choppy trading.

In Seoul, the Kospi recovered from early losses to end 70 points, or 1.39 percent, higher on a rebound by chipmakers, with Samsung Electronics rising 1.13 percent and SK Hynix gaining 3.41 percent. (Agencies)

articles.title: CE builds on Peru trade ties in Fujimori meeting
articles.excerpt: Chief Executive John Lee continued a series of bilateral meetings on Thursday on the sidelines of the Apec summit in…
articles.fullText:
Chief Executive John Lee continued a series of bilateral meetings on Thursday on the sidelines of the Apec summit in Shenzhen.

On the final day of the Apec Economic Leaders’ Meeting, he met with Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori and congratulated her on her successful election in July.

Lee told her he visited Lima two years ago when Peru hosted Apec and the two economies signed a free trade agreement (FTA).

“Trade has, since our signing of the FTA, increased a lot by a double digit in one year so it is very good news, and Hong Kong now regards Peru as a very close trading partner,” he said.

“Peru now is Hong Kong's sixth largest trading partner in Latin America. It amounted to US$600 million, but I think we can have even much room for further promoting it.”

Lee added that negotiations between the two governments have also been active and hopes more agreements will be signed going forward.

He also extended a standing invitation to the Peruvian leader to visit Hong Kong.

Fujimori said she would like to sign additional cooperation agreements on finance and logistics, given that these are areas of SAR expertise.

articles.title: Xi says China-US ties 'generally stable and positive'
articles.excerpt: President Xi Jinping on Thursday said that China-US relations have generally maintained a stable and positive trajectory, injecting stability and…
articles.fullText:
President Xi Jinping on Thursday said that China-US relations have generally maintained a stable and positive trajectory, injecting stability and certainty into the world.

The president made the remarks when meeting with his US counterpart Donald Trump on the sidelines of the Apec summit in Shenzhen.

Xi said that he and Trump had jointly explored the right way for China and the United States, as two major countries, to get along, established a new positioning of a constructive bilateral relationship of strategic stability and given it new meaning based on respect, fairness and reciprocity, according to Xinhua News Agency.

The new positioning has been welcomed by the people of both countries and by the international community, he added.

Trump said the two leaders have jointly guided the development of bilateral relations, and both sides should maintain the positive momentum of the stable development in ties.

Xi also said the US "must keep doing the right thing" on Taiwan to avoid setbacks in ties with Beijing.

"On the Taiwan issue, the United States must keep doing the right thing to avoid the emergence of great turbulence in the China-US relationship," Xinhua quoted Xi as saying.

Trump told Xi that Washington does not support "Taiwan independence".

On artificial intelligence, Xi told his US counterpart that the two countries should cooperate to keep AI "under human control".

"China and the United States should strengthen communication and coordination to guard against artificial intelligence safety risks and ensure that artificial intelligence always remains under human control," Xi said. (Additional reporting by AFP)

Edited by Edmond Fong

articles.title: Xi, Putin, Trump kick off landmark trilateral talks
articles.excerpt: The leaders of China, Russia and the United States have opened historic three-way talks aimed at safeguarding world peace. The…
articles.fullText:
The leaders of China, Russia and the United States have opened historic three-way talks aimed at safeguarding world peace.

The meeting between Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump was held on Thursday afternoon in Shenzhen on the sidelines of the Apec summit.

In his opening remarks, Xi said the first-ever face-to-face meeting between the Chinese, Russian and US heads of state is of groundbreaking significance.

"As major countries in the world and permanent members of the United Nations Security Council, our three countries should set a good example, cooperate in responding to global challenges, jointly safeguard world peace and stability, and make greater contributions to human progress," he said.

Xi also said peace among major countries brings stability to the world, while their contention would only lead to chaos.

He made four points on how major countries could find the right way to get along and jointly underpin world peace – they should uphold mutual respect, peaceful coexistence, win-win cooperation, and dialogue and consultation.

Putin said their three nations shared an "interest" in resolving the Ukraine war and a "responsibility" for global peace and security.

Trump said the three leaders were "making history" by holding talks in Shenzhen.

The trilateral meeting came after Trump held separate one-on-one talks with Putin and Xi earlier in the day.

The wars in Iran and Ukraine as well as nuclear disarmament are expected to be on the agenda. (Xinhua and agencies)

Chief Executive John Lee on Thursday outlined five outcomes for the SAR at this year’s Apec meetings in Shenzhen.

They are: contributing Hong Kong's strengths by actively participating in and supporting the country's successful hosting of the Apec meetings; deepening exchanges and cooperation with Apec member economies; consolidating relations with Asean member states; further exploring emerging markets; and telling the good stories of the Greater Bay Area.

"My takeaway is that Hong Kong's development resonates with our country's development. As an international city and international financial centre, we can serve the country's needs with our unique advantages and what Hong Kong does best," Lee said.

"We are pressing ahead with four centres development and one hub development, contributing to our country's high-quality development. Therefore, we shall actively integrate with and serve our national development, and at the same time, we will strengthen our connectivity with the international world."

Lee noted that he met leaders from a number of Apec member economies through bilateral meetings.

On Wednesday, he met with the leaders of Malaysia, Vietnam, Brunei, Thailand and Chile, and is set to hold talks with leaders from Peru and Singapore on Thursday afternoon.

The CE said he has briefed them on opportunities within the Greater Bay Area, with the talks focusing on strengthening bilateral ties and addressing topics of mutual concern.

Lee said during his meeting with the president of Chile, they jointly witnessed the signing of a Working Holiday Scheme agreement between the two sides, the first of its kind between the SAR and Latin America.

Lee added that the opportunity to meet five Asean leaders would boost Hong Kong's bid to join the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership.

The chief executive also noted that he held a brief conversation with President Xi Jinping, updating him on the panel discussion regarding the Greater Bay Area at the Apec CEO Summit.

Lee said he told Xi the session received a very positive response, with participants agreeing on the massive opportunities available across the region.

Lee said he assured the president that Hong Kong will continue to serve as a "super-connector" and "super value-adder" to better serve and integrate into national development.

articles.title: Arrests over HK$68m phone 'scams'
articles.excerpt: One hundred and twenty-three people have been arrested as police busted two scam call operation centres in a crackdown on…
articles.fullText:
One hundred and twenty-three people have been arrested as police busted two scam call operation centres in a crackdown on phone scams and money laundering, with the cases involving about HK$68 million.

The two-week operation, led by the Commercial Crime Bureau, began in early November.

Of those arrested, 95 were men and the rest women, with their ages ranging between 14 and 75.

Most were stooge account holders or phone registrants and were arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to defraud and obtaining property by deception and money laundering, police said, adding that officers froze HK$1.8 million.

Officers said one of the scam call operation centres was hidden in industrial units in Kwun Tong and Hung Hom.

A 47-year-old man was arrested and two SIM card modems, known as "cat pools", were seized.

Chief Inspector Ho Ming-wai said the use of such device had made the criminal chain highly fragmented and harder to investigate.

"Take the cat pool device at the scene as an example," she said.

"It can dial more than 200 different phone numbers within one hour. Once a citizen answers, the incoming call will be routed through a network system to a phone scam center at another location, continuing this fraudulent activity."

The bureau said phone scams have been rising, with nearly 10,000 cases recorded in the first three quarters of 2026, making up about 30 percent of all cons.

A single-month record of more than 2,000 cases was logged in August, while total losses reached HK$1.9 billion. Impersonation of customer service staff accounted for 60 percent of cases.

Officers also noted scammers are increasingly using two- and three-prefix numbers that look like landlines, when they are actually internet calls, to lower the public's guard.

"These fixed-line phone numbers are, actually, internet calls," Superintendent Kwok Ching-yee said.

"At this stage, they are not yet subject to real-name registration regulation like phone cards and stored-value cards."

In a separate operation, the West Kowloon regional technology and financial crime unit targeted a group impersonating Alipay customer services in an operation that dismantled a call transfer centre.

Thirty-three victims have been defrauded of HK$4 million since December, and police said more arrests are possible.

Edited by Edmond Fong

articles.title: Could caviar served on gourmet food tour of North Korea violate UN sanctions?
articles.excerpt: Russian tour company offers a tour of high-end Pyongyang restaurants inaccessible to average North Koreans.
articles.fullText:
Read a version of this story in Korean .
Caviar, wine, and foie gras served to Russian tourists in high-end Pyongyang restaurants is not necessarily evidence that exporters are violating sanctions that prohibit luxury items shipments to North Korea, but in the spirit of the sanctions these should be considered luxury items, a former member of the U.N. sanctions committee told Radio Free Asia.
Russian travel agency Vostok Intur is offering a gourmet tour that includes meals at many of the places frequented by North Korean elites: the twin-tower Koryo Hotel; the iconic Okryu-gwan restaurant, ground zero for Pyongyang’s high-class food culture; and a cruise ship sailing down the Taedong River which runs through the city.
The Russian Union of Travel Industry reported Monday that the travel company had completed its first gourmet tour with each participant paying roughly US$2,000 for the experience. The tour package includes an itinerary visiting restaurants inaccessible on standard tours, Inna Mukhina, the director of the travel agency, said in the report. The tour route and the restaurants are approved by North Korean tourism authorities, and it includes a stop at a restaurant called Rungra, where caviar and foie gras is served.
A table setting at a high-end Pyongyang restaurant, released by Vostok Intour, a travel agency based in Vladivostok, Russia.
(Vostok Intur) But whether this is a violation of sanctions depends on the interpretation of U.N. resolution 1718 – adopted by the U.N. Security Council in 2006 as a means to prevent the flow of cash and resources into North Korea’s nuclear missile programs. The resolution lists 14 luxury items that are banned for sale to North Korea, but caviar and foie gras are not among them.
The sanctions document should be viewed broadly rather than narrowly, Shuji Sue, a former member of the U.N. Panel of Experts on North Korea sanctions, told RFA Tuesday.
“Because the luxury goods are not specifically exemplified, this has always been a subject of debate when the panel of experts drafts reports,” he said. “I reiterate that I view caviar as a luxury item and consider it to be a luxury product prohibited by the Security Council.”
The European Union designates caviar and its substitutes as prohibited luxury goods, and the U.K., Japan, and Singapore also ban the export of caviar to North Korea. Wine is also subject to the luxury goods export ban by the E.U., the U.S., and the U.K.
Vostok Intur plans to regularize gourmet tourism starting in 2027, once a month with a maximum of 10 people per trip. According to the itinerary released on the agency’s website, tourists will visit the Koryo Hotel restaurant, the Hwasong Kumgang restaurant at the top of the Pyongyang Clock Tower, the Taedong River floating restaurant, and Okryu-gwan.
The price of next year’s group tour package announced by the travel agency is approximately US$1,100, which includes a basic cost of 45,000 rubles (about US$550) plus US$550 for local accommodation expenses. Meal costs are calculated separately.
Even if the sanctions resolution is interpreted broadly, the caviar would not be a violation if it were produced domestically. RFA asked Vostok Intur about the source of the ingredients, but they did not respond.
Domestic production?
Though the source of the caviar has not been confirmed, North Korea has been farming sturgeon since the reign of Kim Jong Il, the father and predecessor of current leader Kim Jong Un. The state-run Korean Central News Agency reported in 2013 that the younger Kim visited a fish farm in South Hwanghae province, and said that his father’s last order before he died in 2011 was to raise as many sturgeon as possible so they could be prepared and served at Okryu-gwan.
This undated picture released by North Korea's official Korean Central News Agency on Feb. 21, 2017 shows North Korean leader Kim Jong-Un visiting the Samchon catfish farm in South Hwanghae Province, North Korea.
(KCNA via AFP) RFA was not able to confirm whether North Korea produces caviar domestically, but if it does, it can only be in small quantities, Lee Hyunseung, a former member of the North Korean elite whose family fled North Korea in 2014 and who now resides in the United States, told RFA.
“We cannot confirm the exact production volume, but as long as fish farms exist, domestic production is possible,” said Lee, who works as a senior researcher at the Maryland-based Global Peace Foundation. “However, mass production is not feasible. Clearly, if the number of tourists increases and tourism programs are operated more frequently, imports would be necessary to guarantee the required quantity.”
China is the world’s largest producer and exporter of sturgeon caviar but Beijing’s official export statistics show no record of the delicacy being sent to North Korea between 2018 and 2025. Russia, meanwhile, has not disclosed bilateral trade statistics since 2022, meaning that potentially Chinese caviar could enter North Korea via Russia.
Inequality exposed
The gourmet food tours are a stark contrast to the lifestyles of the typical resident of North Korea, a country that struggles with chronic food shortages, where a month’s salary cannot even buy a bag of rice.
Lee said that restaurants such as the Koryo Hotel or the Taedong River cruise ship can cost up to hundreds of dollars for a single meal, making them inaccessible to most people living in North Korea.
RFA reported last month that an average factory worker earns 20,000 North Korean won, about 30 US cents at the market exchange rate.
According to Vostok Intur’s itineraries, the tourists’ lunches and dinners are ordered and paid for separately, with an average cost of US$20 per meal. This amount is equivalent to approximately five and a half times the average worker’s annual salary.
A group of Russian tourists arrive at the Pyongyang International Airport in Pyongyang, North Korea, Friday, Feb. 9, 2024.
(Cha Song Ho/AP) “ Russians travel to North Korea like this, pay US$2,000, and enjoy a luxurious trip for three nights and four days,” said Lee. “I wonder how many people in North Korea can actually afford to pay US$2,000 and enjoy that kind of luxury. Even the wealthy elites in the country simply cannot spend like that.”
According to South Korea’s Ministry of Unification, the cash-strapped North Korean government regards tourism as a key means of earning badly needed foreign currency.
“These tourism profits will also eventually be handed over to Kim Jong Un through the General Administration of National Tourism,” said Lee.
Edited by Yi Yongin in Korean and Eugene Whong in English.

articles.title: Foreign reporters enjoy their stays in Shenzhen
articles.excerpt: Media professionals gathered in Shenzhen for this year’s Apec meetings have had high praise for the city, hailing its technology…
articles.fullText:
Media professionals gathered in Shenzhen for this year’s Apec meetings have had high praise for the city, hailing its technology and people's hospitality.

Ekaterini Nicolaou from Cyprus, who is in China for the first time, said she was deeply touched by the hospitality of the locals.

"People are amazing and very hospitable. Even though we don't communicate in English, a lot of the time they're still very helpful and always there," she said.

"I feel very emotional to talk about this because Chinese people are impressive with their hospitality.

"We are in the subway, and somebody without you even asking them, they come to you and say, ‘Can I help you?’ and they don't take the train.'

She was also impressed by the humanoid robots showcased at the media centre, particularly those serving as TV hosts.

Sodas Salih from Iraq shared the same sentiment, saying he was impressed with the high-tech cameras showcased at the media centre.

"I think it’s like a letter from the Chinese government to tell the world that Shenzhen is special and Shenzhen is a capital of AI and technology, and they want the world to understand that Shenzhen is a special city," he said.

Alicia Boucher from Trinidad and Tobago was equally impressed by the China’s advancements in robotics.

"I have seen a lot of robots. My favourite, though, are humanoids," she said.

"I think it can be a great emotional support tool for a lot of people, the economic landscape, the cost of living."

Jarryl Bryan from Guyana, a coastal country in South America, was impressed by the amenities provided to help foreign reporters settle in.

"I've noticed that there are a lot of bilingual services, and I think it’s great. Everybody is accommodating all the foreign journalists here to cover Apec and so on,” he said.

The media centre also offers halal food and prayer rooms, alongside cleansing facilities in the washrooms for Muslim visitors.

According to Madiha Abid from Pakistan, the inclusion of halal options is a move that's very well thought-out.

"I think this is very sensitive, only a very considerate person could think like this. We have to respect the people who only eat halal, and they are offering a halal buffet. I'm very thankful to the management of Apec,” she said.

Diana Arushanyan from Armenia said she loved how China brought people from different cultural backgrounds together.

“I really love the idea that China is helping not only communicating with different cultures, but also making different cultures communicate with each other, and work to build something new,” she said.

Spanning 15,000 square metres, the media centre is capable of accommodating nearly 5,000 reporters.

Edited by Edmond Fong

articles.title: HK slips as Anthropic IPO to hold clue to AI sentiment
articles.excerpt: Asian equities were mixed and US stock futures rose on Thursday after Claude chatbot maker Anthropic scored the biggest initial…
articles.fullText:
Asian equities were mixed and US stock futures rose on Thursday after Claude chatbot maker Anthropic scored the biggest initial public offering ever with an US$81 billion offering ahead of its market debut in a test for the artificial intelligence trade that has been under pressure in recent weeks.

In Hong Kong, the benchmark Hang Seng Index opened down 245 points, or 1.05 percent, at 23,049.

The China enterprises index slid 74 points, or 0.95 percent, to 7,762 while the tech index fell 36 points, or 0.97 percent, to 3,699.

Higher north, the benchmark Shanghai Composite Index inched down four points, or 0.13 percent, to open at 3,583.

The Shenzhen Component Index fell 67 points, or 0.63 percent, to 10,591 while the ChiNext Index was down 0.93 percent at 2,290.

In Tokyo, the Nikkei opened less than a point up at 59,025 and was 136 points higher at one stage before lunch.

In Seoul, the Kospi rose 22 points, or 0.45 percent, to open at 5,090 before reversing direction to be 67 points lower at one stage before lunch.

On a fully diluted basis, Anthropic's IPO values the large language model maker, the first major frontier AI model developer to go public, at about US$1.5 trillion and its first-day trading will be scrutinised to gauge investor sentiment on the technology.

Kyle Rodda, senior financial market analyst at Capital.com, said it was going to be a huge test for the markets and it looked poised to be a really bullish listing.

"I don't think it's necessarily going to assuage all the fears about AI. I think much of that boils down to future investment growth... However, if the stock trades the way it looks like it will, it might calm the market a bit."

Investor confidence in AI has been shaken in the past few weeks on worries about the profitability of the technology and the massive debt needed to fund and build AI infrastructure.

Markets mostly shrugged off a strong forecast from chipmaker Nvidia this week as uncertainty caused by chief executive Jensen Huang's departure last week rattled investors. The company's board dismissed the idea of rehiring Huang.

In currencies, the dollar was on the front foot as hawkish comments from US Federal Reserve governor Christopher Waller bolstered expectations of an interest rate hike in December.

Waller said on CNBC that if the central bank wanted to get inflation down it needed to take more "aggressive action" either through a half-point increase at the December meeting, or by using the post-meeting statement to set market expectations for further hikes.

The comments come after hotter-than-expected inflation data last week, leaving markets bracing for a rate hike. Traders are pricing in a 90 percent chance of a 25 basis points hike next month, the CME FedWatch tool showed.

"More hawkish Fed pricing has so far offset weakness in technology stocks, keeping the USD supported," OCBC strategists said in a note. "Persistent inflation, further Fed tightening and elevated US yields suggest it is still too early to bet against the USD." (Agencies)

Edited by Edmond Fong

articles.title: China pledges US$20m to boost Apec cooperation: Xi
articles.excerpt: President Xi Jinping on Thursday called on leaders attending the Apec summit in Shenzhen to build an Asia-Pacific community that…
articles.fullText:
President Xi Jinping on Thursday called on leaders attending the Apec summit in Shenzhen to build an Asia-Pacific community that features solidarity and mutual assistance, openness and integration, innovation, and inclusive development.

Xi said China will provide US$20 million to support regional cooperation at the Apec Economic Leaders' Meeting, as he announced a series of measures to consistently support cooperation across the Asia-Pacific.

These include the establishment of a centre for Asia-Pacific community studies in Shenzhen to conduct policy research and exchanges and provide intellectual support.

The president said China will also set up cooperation institutions in such areas as digital technology, cross-border data flow, clean energy and the development of small and medium-sized enterprises, contributing to innovation-driven and green growth in the Asia-Pacific.

Xi also stressed the need to steadily advance economic integration in the region, and called on members to facilitate free, open trade and investment, unclog bottlenecks and ensure smooth economic circulation.

He emphasised the importance of innovation in building an Asia-Pacific community, saying it is imperative to encourage exchanges and cooperation on the sci-tech front, facilitate the utilisation of innovation outcomes, and foster a cooperation environment that is open, fair, just and non-discriminatory.

Xi added that the bond of shared interests among Apec members should be strengthened, and they should work together to tackle difficulties and challenges, and continue to foster a sense of community.

Efforts should be made to ensure that the benefits of development are shared by all, he said.

China is an advocate, promoter and forerunner in Asia-Pacific economic cooperation, Xi added, saying China is ready to work with all parties to build the pillars that support an Asia-Pacific community. (Reporting by Xinhua)
